html:
The Laurel complex was a Woodland culture of the lakes and forests of the western Great Lakes, in what is now northern Minnesota, northwestern Wisconsin, northern Michigan, much of Ontario, east central Manitoba and southern Quebec. Its people were the first to make pottery in Ontario north of the Trent and Severn waterway.

Laurel people lived by hunting, fishing and gathering, moving with the seasons through lake and river country. Their pots were cone shaped and marked with stamped and dotted bands. In the south of their range they built burial mounds; the largest is Grand Mound on the Rainy River in Minnesota.

The complex takes its name from the former community of Laurel, Minnesota, and was first defined by the archaeologist Lloyd Wilford in 1941. It sat on the northern edge of the mound building world shaped by the Hopewell exchange. Some archaeologists see Laurel people among the ancestors of later Algonquian speakers such as the Cree and Ojibwe. To the east lived the Point Peninsula people.
